Photograph: Mark Kolbe/Getty Images Sydney Sydney man who allegedly called 13-year-old Muslim girl a ‘terrorist’ berates judge after bail refused Omar Yassine was arrested and charged with stalking and intimidation after allegedly hurling insults at year 8 student wearing a hijab Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian Associated Press Wed 16 Sep 2026 01.27 EDT Last modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 01.45 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A middle-aged man accused of a “disgusting” Islamophobic attack on a 13-year-old girl has berated a judge after he was denied bail Omar Yassine made an eventful court appearance on Wednesday after being held by police overnight for allegedly verbally abusing the Muslim schoolgirl on a Sydney bus. Yassine told the court he had “hurled a few insults” at the girl, her friends and someone he thought was a teacher on Thursday but claimed he had not been the instigator. “I didn’t threaten or intimidate anyone,” the 50-year-old, who did not want legal representation, said from the Bankstown local court dock on Wednesday. “All I did was raise my phone ... a person alleged I took a photo [of them]. “There were four students hurling threats and abuse at me.” The police prosecutor said there was strong evidence against Yassine, who the court heard had a 46-page criminal record. The evidence included a video, recorded by the 13-year-old girl on an inner-western Sydney bus, that showed Yassine calling her a barrage of names, the prosecutor said. The year 8 student, who was wearing a hijab and her school uniform, was allegedly called a “fucking terrorist” and an “immigrant dog” among other insults in the clip, later shared online. The girl and other passengers reported the tirade to police after getting off the bus at Strathfield station. Officers arrested Yassine at a home in nearby Greenacre after the girl and her mother went public about the incident on Tuesday. He was charged with stalking and intimidation with intent to cause fear. In the video, the teen told the man she was born in Australia and reminded him of her young age, but that didn’t stop the alleged abuse. The girl and her mother told the ABC the incident was “really disgusting”. In court, Yassine repeatedly interrupted the police prosecutor and acting judge Gary Still. The 50-year-old said he should be released on bail because he would be able to report to police and was not a risk of committing another serious offence. Judge Still disagreed. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “This is a vulnerable victim, a 13-year-old on public transport,” the judge said. “There are a number of matters on your record ... and you are just off a community corrections order.” Upon being refused bail, Yassine turned his disdain on the judge. “You’re pre-empting my behaviour ... how did you come up with that conclusion?” Yassine said as he was led off to the cells. “Good work, Your Honour – bow down to them, mate.” The abuse allegedly began after the 13-year-old stood up for another girl in a hijab who believed Yassine was taking photos of her without her knowledge. The Strathfield state MP Jason Yat-sen Li said he was “horrified and deeply angry” about the alleged incident, while congratulating the teen for speaking up. “Let me be absolutely clear: Strathfield will not tolerate racist or Islamophobic abuse, particularly when it targets children,” he said. Yassine was not required to enter a plea and will return to court at a later date. https://www.politico.eu/article/ursula-v.text: BRUSSELS ― Ursula von der Leyen used a major speech on Wednesday to pitch Europe as the leader of a group of like-minded countries that want to hold their own against rival powers such as Russia and China. Not invited to join this EU-led coalition? Donald Trump’s United States. Speaking before an audience that included Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has publicly fallen out with Trump, the European Commission president spelled out her vision of Europe as a geopolitical leader with plans for new partnerships and closer relationships — the most notable of which was offering to explore possible “associate EU membership” status for Canada, in what would amount to a major first for the EU. Advertisement Advertisement “In this new world, we must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said in the speech at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg. She added that the EU wanted to “build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies. And here too only Europe ― with its size and power ― can take the lead.” For the head of the EU’s executive branch, who’s now two years into her second five-year term, the speech amounted to a declaration of geopolitical legacy. Coming one year after she declared Europe’s “independence moment” from the same platform, von der Leyen expanded on that idea in a speech that seemed to echo Carney’s own address at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in which he called for the world’s “middle powers” to stand together against autocrats. Ursula von der Leyen delivers her annual State of the Union address at a plenary session of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France on Sept. 16, 2026. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images In addition to offering Canada associate member status, von der Leyen suggested bringing the leaders of the U.K., Norway, Canada and Ukraine together in a newfangled “European Security Council” that would exist outside of NATO, offering a platform to discuss hybrid threats without the United States. She also proposed that, with Europe in the role of coordinator, like-minded countries could jointly address challenges ranging from climate change to Chinese industrial overcapacity to the risks of frontier AI models. “This speech was all about the big threats occupying European leaders: Russia and China, and to a lesser extent the United States,” said Mujtaba Rahman, Europe director at the Eurasia Group political consultancy. “It was all about how the EU can organize itself amid an imperialist Russia, a withdrawing America and a materialist China — it’s an attempt to draw those dots together.” Advertisement Advertisement Yet for many of those watching, the speech was heavy on lofty ideas like associate membership for Canada — which faces considerable obstacles to become a reality — and light on practical new proposals to deal with Europe’s immediate challenges. “Dr. von der Leyen is at her best when she diagnoses the ills of our time and of our Europe,” said French centrist lawmaker Nathalie Loiseau, who sits on the European Parliament’s security and defense committee. “We’re still waiting for the prescription that will help Europe regain its health.” Skating over the issues At a time when the EU economy is struggling with anemic growth and high inflation linked to runaway energy prices, the Commission president reiterated previously announced policy proposals on the economy, rather than pitching new ideas. For example, the speech did not address how to meet Ukraine’s immediate financing needs — a pressing concern at a time when Kyiv has said it needs an additional €23 billion before the end of the year and the EU is its main financial benefactor. It also included tough language on trade imbalances with China and the toll they are taking on Europe’s economy, but included no new policy proposal aside from doubling down on ongoing dialogue with Beijing. It also skated over some of the major foreign policy issues dividing EU capitals, namely the Middle East and Israel’s relationship with the Palestinian territories in the West Bank and Gaza. Advertisement Advertisement Von der Leyen made headlines last year by proposing to suspend the EU’s Association Agreement with Israel over humanitarian violations in Gaza. But this time she disappointed lawmakers who’d hoped she might offer a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements, an implicit recognition that her proposal from last year had floundered amid divisions between capitals. Instead, she lamented the situation in Israel’s illegal West Bank settlements — and urged governments to overcome their disagreements. Most of all, however, it was von der Leyen’s implicit suggestion that the EU should forge on without relying on the U.S., striking up new partnerships and setting up its own Security Council — outside of NATO — that seemed to unnerve some of the diplomats, lawmakers and officials watching her speech. “I think it is a very bad idea. I think that it gives the signal to the world that NATO is irrelevant and we need to replace it with something,” said Riho Terras. | Denis Lomme/EP “I think it is a very bad idea. I think that it gives the signal to the world that NATO is irrelevant and we need to replace it with something,” said Riho Terras, an Estonian member of the conservative European People’s Party and former commander of his country’s armed forces. “Putin is talking about recreating the security infrastructure in Europe and now the European Union starts to do it itself by attacking NATO.” The Security Council was “a dead-born idea,” said Željana Zovko, vice-chair of von der Leyen’s EPP. Indeed, many watchers pointed to the reality that in areas ranging from technology to pharmaceuticals to defense procurement, the EU remains heavily dependent on the U.S. “So much of what we need for Europe’s defense and our economy is done with the United States,” said a diplomat from an eastern EU country who was granted anonymity. “Why alienate them?” Max Griera contributed reporting from Strasbourg.
